title: Network lab 4: VLANs for staff and guests (Packet Tracer)
summary: Split one switch into a staff VLAN and a guest VLAN with real switch commands, and prove that guests can't reach staff computers.

script.intro: Welcome to network lab four, and to Cisco Packet Tracer. Packet Tracer is Cisco's own teaching simulator, so the commands you type are the real ones from the operating system on Cisco switches and routers. The scene moves to Tulsi Travels, a travel agent with one twenty-four port switch in its front office. Staff computers and the customers waiting on the sofa all plug into that same switch, and they must not share a network. We'll split the switch into two VLANs, staff and guest, with the same commands you'd type on a real switch, and then prove a visitor can't reach staff, even by guessing an address.
script.outro: Remember three things from today. A VLAN splits one switch into separate networks. The port decides which VLAN a device is in, not its address. And separation you haven't tested against an attacker's guess is only a hope. See you in lab five.

steps.say: Step one: install Packet Tracer and build the office. Packet Tracer is free, but you need a Cisco Networking Academy account. Sign up at netacad.com, enrol in the free course Getting Started with Cisco Packet Tracer, and download it from the course page. Then place one 2960 switch and four PCs, and cable them with Copper Straight-Through to the ports in README.txt: staff-1 and staff-2 on Fa0/1 and Fa0/2, guest-1 and guest-2 on Fa0/13 and Fa0/14. On each PC, open Desktop, then IP Configuration, and type its address with netmask 255.255.255.0.
steps.after: Watch the link lights. They start amber and turn green after a few seconds, while the switch checks the new link. Wait for green before you test anything. Fa0/1 means FastEthernet, slot 0, port 1, and you'll type names like that all through these labs. Straight-through is the normal cable between a computer and a switch, so that's the answer.

steps.say: Step two: make the VLANs. Click the switch and open the CLI tab. Type enable, then configure terminal. Create VLAN 10 and name it STAFF, then VLAN 20 and name it GUEST. Then use interface range to make ports 1 to 12 access ports in VLAN 10, and ports 13 to 20 access ports in VLAN 20. Type end, then show vlan brief.
steps.after: show vlan brief prints one line per VLAN with its ports. VLAN 10, STAFF, owns Fa0/1 to Fa0/12. VLAN 20, GUEST, owns Fa0/13 to Fa0/20. Ports 21 to 24 and both gigabit ports are still in VLAN 1, the default. That's fine for now, and lab six deals with them. An access port belongs to exactly one VLAN, and the computer plugged into it has no idea VLANs exist: it just sees a network. Why 10 and 20? Any number from 2 to 1001 works on this switch, but matching the VLAN to the third number of the address, 10 for 192.168.10, makes the plan easy to read. The command that lists every VLAN and its ports is show vlan brief.

steps.say: Step three: prove the separation. On staff-1, open Command Prompt. Ping staff-2 at 192.168.10.12, then guest-1 at 192.168.20.31. Then the real test. Change guest-1's address to 192.168.10.99, as if a visitor guessed the staff range and typed it in, and from guest-1, ping staff-1.
steps.after: Staff to staff answers. Staff to guest fails, but on its own that proves little: they're in different IP networks with no router, so it would fail without any VLANs. The guessed address is the proof. guest-1 now has an address in the staff network, and still nothing gets through, because the switch never forwards a frame from a VLAN 20 port out of a VLAN 10 port. Picking an address doesn't move you into another VLAN; the switch port decides. That's why security teams like VLANs: the switch enforces the rule, not the person choosing settings. A visitor can change anything on their own laptop, but not the switch's configuration. They could still move their cable to a staff wall port, and lab six closes that gap too. Put guest-1's address back. The answers are no, and the switch port.

steps.say: That's lab four: one switch, two separate networks. But guests still need the internet, and that means a router. In lab five we join the VLANs on purpose, through a router we control.
